#Tech industry

  • Big Tech's AI capex hits an estimated $725B for 2026, up roughly 77 percent, as free cash flow across the top hyperscalers is projected to approach zero by Q3: Earnings season is now the referee. Alphabet reports July 22 and Microsoft July 29, and Wall Street is explicitly demanding "receipts", proof that the spend converts to revenue, with Azure growth below 35 percent likely read as a severe deceleration. Strategic implication: the market is shifting from rewarding AI ambition to pricing AI ROI. Expect vendors to reprice, bundle, and push consumption-based contracts harder in H2 to show monetization. If you are a buyer, this is leverage. If you are a builder, the bar on demonstrating payback just moved up.

#AI at the leadership level

The adoption-to-governance gap is now the defining board risk. Roughly 55 percent of enterprises are actively deploying AI, but only 26 percent say their governance frameworks are fully aligned with that pace, and while ~41 percent are already running agentic AI in production, only about 15 percent say they are fully prepared to. Directors are convening specifically on oversight: not whether AI works, but how fast to move and where value diverges from risk. The CDO mandate is visibly shifting from data stewardship toward enterprise risk operator, owning AI dependency maps, decision-chain documentation, and cross-functional governance boards. Board takeaway: the competitive question in 2026 is no longer "are we using AI" but "can we govern it fast enough to keep deploying it," because the first serious incident is what stalls adoption, not the technology.

#Leadership & org design

"Forward Deployed Engineering" is hardening into an operating model, not a buzzword. Microsoft committed $2.5B and 6,000 employees to embed engineers directly inside client operations, two days after Amazon put $1B behind a similar FDE initiative, with Anthropic and OpenAI having stood up FDE groups earlier this year. The signal for org-builders: value is moving to the teams that sit inside the customer's workflow and ship in their context, not the ones that sell a license and leave. Meanwhile, AI-cited restructurings (a fintech cutting ~20 percent of headcount over two to three years, others explicitly redeploying people into AI roles) show the reorganization is real, not rhetorical. Practical move: audit where your highest-value talent sits relative to the customer's actual work, and consider whether your best people are close enough to the point of use to compound.

#Question worth asking your team this week

If our biggest AI vendor had to prove payback to us the way Wall Street is forcing them to prove it this earnings season, which of our current AI deployments would survive that review, and which are we funding on faith?

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • LinkedIn AI ad variants + Brand Kit: Campaign Manager now has Draft with AI, Brand Kit, and AI ad variants live for all advertisers. Load your colors, fonts, tone, and key messages into Brand Kit once so generated creative stays on-brand, then spin up 5+ headline and intro variants per campaign. LinkedIn's own data shows campaigns running five or more variants get 20%+ higher CTR than single-ad campaigns. Twenty minutes to set the Brand Kit and launch a variant test that would have taken a designer a week.
  • Adobe Advertising Custom Algorithms: Adobe's DSP now trains your bidding model directly on raw Adobe Analytics data instead of the thin slice APIs usually pass through. The lever for practitioners is defining High Value Actions (video views, newsletter signups, checkout steps) so the model optimizes toward real engagement signals, not just last-click conversions. Worth doing this week if you have meaningful first-party traffic and are tired of renting Google/Meta's black-box optimization. This one bids on your data without owning the inventory.
  • PRD-to-prototype one-pager: Instead of a full PRD, write a focused one-pager (user, goal, success criteria, failure modes) and hand it to an AI prototyping tool to generate a clickable prototype in hours. Teams doing this report 30-50% less time from concept to testable artifact. Run one this week on a stalled backlog item and put a real prototype in front of five users before the next sprint planning.

#Case study worth stealing

EQUIVA, omnichannel loyalty at the center: The retailer rebuilt around loyalty optimization as the connective tissue between online and store, rather than treating the program as a points bolt-on. Result: 23% lift in average transaction value and 42% more transactions per customer. The adaptable part for any digital team is sequencing, they made loyalty the data spine that identifies and personalizes across channels, so every touchpoint feeds the same profile. If your loyalty program lives in a silo next to the CRM, this is the argument for wiring it into the identity layer instead.

#Framework or mental model

Product judgment over documentation: As AI makes code cheap, prototypes fast, and docs trivial to generate, the scarce skill moves upstream to deciding what is worth building, what ships first, and what gets ignored. The "product builder" is whoever can move from insight to working artifact fastest and let real feedback, not files, measure progress. Digital leaders should re-weight their teams and their own week toward judgment calls and user tests, and stop rewarding volume of specs.

#Rabbit hole (optional)

The PM role is visibly splitting in 2026. Hands-on "product builders" who ship prototypes are separating from the broader strategy-and-alignment remit, and the consensus is that strategy and business acumen, not tool fluency, are the durable skills for the next two to three years. Worth thinking about how you structure your team as AI collapses the execution layer: fewer people writing PRDs, more people owning outcomes end to end.

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • Publicis Groupe / LiveRamp: Publicis is acquiring identity and data-collaboration vendor LiveRamp for roughly $2.2B all-cash ($38.50/share, a ~30% premium). Signal: A holdco is buying the identity spine rather than renting it. The pitch is "data co-creation" across brands and publishers without leaning on US platform gatekeepers. When an agency group vertically integrates the identity resolution layer, it reframes identity from a neutral utility every DSP taps into a strategic asset one buyer controls. Everyone downstream should re-examine whether their identity partner is now a competitor's asset.
  • Salesforce Agentforce Commerce: Shopper, Buyer, and Merchant agents are now generally available, with native integration into ChatGPT and Google (AI Mode, Gemini) arriving in coming months. Signal: The commerce surface is moving off owned properties and into third-party AI assistants. If a Buyer Agent transacts inside ChatGPT, the retailer's site stops being the funnel and the martech job shifts from optimizing a page to feeding structured product and inventory data into agents you do not own.
  • 6sense MCP Server (open beta): 6sense buying-intent data is now callable from any MCP-compatible agent (Claude, ChatGPT, Writer, Agentforce), GA targeted for August. Signal: Model Context Protocol is becoming the integration pattern that replaces bespoke API connectors. Vendors that expose their data as an MCP endpoint make themselves consumable by whatever agent a customer already runs, which is a defense against being locked out of a rival's walled agent ecosystem.

#Category watch

Agentic CRM and engagement: The race to rebuild the suite around persistent agents is now the whole competitive field, not a feature. Salesforce, Adobe (Experience Cloud rebranded to CX Enterprise with agent "Coworkers"), and HubSpot are all repositioning from tool-centric software to goal-oriented, agent-run workflows. MoEngage buying Aampe to form an "agentic customer engagement platform" shows the same logic hitting mid-market. For anyone building a martech org, the question is shifting from "which tools do we license" to "which agents do we let act autonomously, and on whose data." Only a small fraction of teams run campaigns where multiple agents operate without a human in the loop, so the gap between the vendor narrative and operational reality is wide and worth pressure-testing before you buy the vision.

#Stack intelligence

The token economics of agentic pipelines are quietly forcing an architecture decision. A single daily agent pipeline can burn thousands of tokens per run and exhaust a flat subscription in an afternoon, which pushes cost from predictable SaaS seats to volatile usage. The emerging pattern: keep raw data in a warehouse you own (Snowflake, BigQuery, Postgres) and use cheap non-LLM filtering to select the relevant slice before anything hits the model, cutting token spend by more than half while keeping quality. The strategic framing is "do you want to pay for the work, or own the infrastructure and pay only for the reasoning." This favors warehouse-native, provider-agnostic builds over deep consolidation into one vendor's agent stack, because owning the context layer lets you swap models by config instead of migration.

#Foundations concept of the day

Identity graphs: An identity graph is a database that stitches the many signals a single person leaves behind (emails, device IDs, cookies, loyalty IDs, hashed logins) into one persistent profile, so a customer looks like one person across channels instead of a dozen strangers. It works by matching deterministic keys (a login you know is the same person) and probabilistic ones (same household, same device pattern) into a linked record. Why it matters at scale: with third-party cookies still fading in relevance, the graph built on your own first-party logins is what lets you recognize, target, and measure people across web, app, email, and connected TV. Cross-industry example: a retailer connects in-store loyalty scans to website behavior and app purchases through one graph, so a shopper who browses on mobile and buys in store counts as one journey rather than three disconnected events. This is exactly why LiveRamp commands a $2.2B price and why The Trade Desk is investing in warehouse-activation players like Hightouch. Whoever owns the graph owns the ability to resolve and value an audience.

#Watch list

  • MCP as the martech integration standard: 6sense exposing intent data over Model Context Protocol, alongside Salesforce and Adobe wiring agents into ChatGPT and Gemini, points to MCP becoming the connective tissue between data vendors and agents. If it holds, the moat shifts from proprietary API integrations to whoever owns the underlying data an agent must call. Watch which vendors publish MCP endpoints next.
  • Warehouse-native activation: The Trade Desk's stake in Hightouch (round valuing it at $2.75B, more than double 14 months prior) plus the direct integration piping raw DSP impression logs into brands' own data warehouses signals that activation is moving to the warehouse rather than a separate CDP. Watch whether the standalone CDP category keeps consolidating into data-cloud and DSP ecosystems.

Markets Signal

#Macro pulse

Oil is the story. Canada: TSX fell 0.8% to 34,960 Monday, banks leading the decline as rising oil lifted bond yields, even after a softer-than-expected June inflation print. USD/CAD sits near 1.4070, flat, no international-revenue flag today. USA: risk-off Monday. S&P 500 down 1% to 7,457.69, Nasdaq down 1.4% to 25,520.24, Dow down 0.8% to 52,146.42, an AI-driven chip selloff that spread from semis into broader growth. Meta (+2.8%) and Alphabet (+2.2%) bucked the tape. Asia: rebound Tuesday. Nikkei 225 up 3.26% to 66,232, Hang Seng up 0.09%, Shanghai Composite up 1.28%. Oil: WTI up 1.7% to about $84.60, Brent up 1.8% near $89, both at five-week highs after Yemen's Houthis declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia and fresh US-Iran strikes. This is the airline-margin flag: crude has run hard off geopolitics, jet fuel costs follow.

#Today's industry move

The macro signal for travel and loyalty is the fuel line, not a single ticker. A Houthi blockade threatens Saudi crude that transits pipelines bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, the relief valve the market has counted on. Sustained Brent near $90 pressures carrier cost structures into peak summer demand and tilts the yield-vs-load-factor calculus toward holding fares. For Canadian international routes, a flat loonie means no FX offset on those higher fuel bills.

#AI infrastructure watch

Monday's selloff started in semiconductors before rippling out, a reminder that the AI trade now sets the risk tone for the whole tape. Nothing structural broke: NVIDIA's most recent quarter was $68.1B revenue (up 73%) with $62.3B from data center, AMD data center at $5.8B (up 57%), TSMC May revenue up 30% year over year. The pullback reads as positioning and valuation air (NVIDIA at roughly 43x forward), not a demand crack in the chips-to-data-center stack.

#Signal or noise?

Mostly noise on equities, real signal on oil: the chip wobble is a one-day valuation reset inside an intact buildout, but the Red Sea and Saudi blockade escalation is a genuine new supply front that could keep crude elevated for weeks.

#Watch tomorrow

Whether US-Iran mediation reports firm up or the Saudi blockade hardens. That single headline sets crude, and crude sets the airline cost line for the back half of summer.

item.title: The Platero Brief, No. 24: Monday, July 20, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Executive Pulse

#Macro signal

Energy shock re-prices the entire rate path: A ninth consecutive night of US strikes on Iran and the suspension of the June interim accord pushed Brent to $90.97, up 3.3%, with direct tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz turning a risk premium into a physical supply problem. Swaps traders cut expected 2026 Fed easing to 56 basis points from 60, CME FedWatch now puts an 85.6% probability on no change at the July meeting, and the Bloomberg dollar index jumped 0.8% to its highest since early February. The ECB meets Thursday facing pressure for a second consecutive hike into weak growth, and the PBoC held its one-year rate at 3.0% to defend the yuan rather than stimulate.

The strategic read: the disinflation trade that underwrote every 2026 plan is now conditional on a geopolitical variable no operator controls. If you built next year's budget on a falling cost of capital, that assumption is live again. The dollar surge also quietly tightens conditions for anyone with emerging market revenue or supply exposure, and the IMF's 3.8% emerging market growth forecast carries clear downside from the combination of stronger dollar and higher oil. Leaders should be stress testing the stagflation case, not just the soft landing, and asking which contracts and hedges reset if energy stays above $90 through Q4.

#Tech industry

  • The AI infrastructure trade broke, and it was valuation not fundamentals: The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 11% in a week and is down roughly 24% from its late-June high, formally a bear market, with more than a trillion dollars of market value erased. Three catalysts stacked up: reports that Meta is standing up Meta Compute to resell surplus training and inference capacity, which rewrites the supply side of the AI infrastructure equation; Intel's 18A-P node reportedly not reaching profitable yields until late 2026 or 2027, undercutting a stock that had run 278% in H1; and SK Hynix slowing its high bandwidth memory expansion. Today's session added falling chips, rising oil, and a 10% post-earnings Netflix decline into one move. The implication is not that AI demand is fading, it is that the market has stopped paying in advance for it. Capital allocation committees that waved through AI spend on narrative alone will now be asked for a return schedule.
  • Inference is becoming a commodity input: Grok 4.5, GPT-5.6, and Muse Spark 1.1 all launched inside a 24 hour window, dragging output token pricing into the $4 to $6 range against $25 to $50 for legacy flagships, while mid-tier models approach flagship performance and open-weight options offer a cheaper usage-based route. Any product margin model built on last year's token costs is stale, and any moat premised on model access is gone. The defensible layer is proprietary data, workflow ownership, and distribution, not the model.

#AI at the leadership level

The gap is no longer adoption, it is governance. Board-level AI use has gone near universal, with 92% of directors reporting they used AI for board work in the past six months against 69% a year earlier, but formal oversight has not followed: documented responsibilities, committee assignments, and structured AI risk reporting remain rare. The structural data says the same thing. AI listed as a disclosed risk among S&P 500 companies went from 12% to 83% between 2023 and 2025, yet disclosed board AI expertise crawled from 1.5% to 2.7%, only 23% of executives rate their board as highly fluent in AI, and just 9% call their company very prepared for AI regulatory compliance. Boards are now heavy users of a technology they are not equipped to govern, which is precisely the shape of an incident waiting to be written up. The near-term move is unglamorous: name the owner, define the escalation path, and put AI risk on a reporting cadence before a regulator or an incident defines it for you.

#Leadership & org design

The flattening is moving from rhetoric to filed restructurings, and the interesting part is the design intent rather than the headcount. GitLab paired a 7% workforce reduction with the removal of up to three management layers in some functions and a split of R&D into roughly 60 smaller autonomous teams, explicitly framed as preparation for an agentic era. Coinbase cut to five layers below the CEO and COO and is piloting one-person teams that fold engineering, design, and product into a single role. Bayer, Amazon, and Meta have made comparable public commitments, and roughly 41% of employees say their company trimmed management layers last year.

The logic is specific, not fashionable. Middle management's core function was information routing: decisions down, status up, coordination across. Agents do all three, so the coordination layer compresses and spans of control widen. The trap is cutting the layer without replacing what it actually did, because judgment, context, and talent development were never routing work. Organizations that flatten well are redesigning the decision rights and the information flow first, then removing the layer. Ones that flatten badly are removing the layer and discovering what it was holding.

#Question worth asking your team this week

If oil stays above $90 and the Fed does not cut this year, which three commitments in our current plan stop being fundable, and would we rather choose which ones to kill now or have the number choose for us in October?

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • Claude Fable 5 access rules land today: Anthropic ended three weeks of rolling deadline extensions. As of July 20, Fable 5 is included in Max and Team Premium at 50% of standard weekly limits. Pro and Team Standard drop to usage credits with a one-time $100 grant, after which it bills at API rates of $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. If a team standardized on Fable for high-stakes drafting or analysis while it was effectively free, the unit economics changed overnight. Worth 20 minutes to audit who on the team is on which plan and reroute routine work to Sonnet 5, which sits at $3 in and $15 out after the introductory window closes August 31.
  • SQLite Query Explainer: A browser tool that runs SQLite through Pyodide in WebAssembly, with no backend, and annotates both EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN and the low-level bytecode with plain-English descriptions of what the query planner is actually doing. Useful for analysts and PMs who write SQL against product data but have never been able to read a query plan. Caveat from the builder: the explanations have not been independently verified, so treat them as a learning aid rather than a source of truth.
  • LLM Cliché Highlighter: A single-purpose web app that flags ten recurring tells of machine-generated prose, including constructions like "worth naming" and "is real and." Run marketing copy, exec summaries, and customer-facing content through it before publishing. The practical value is not detection, it is calibration: it shows a team exactly which verbal tics their AI-assisted drafts keep reintroducing, which is the fastest way to build an internal style guard.

#Case study worth stealing

Klarna, the walk-back on AI-first customer service: Klarna's assistant handled 2.3 million conversations in its first month, resolved roughly two-thirds of support tickets, and cut average resolution time from 11 minutes to 2, with an estimated $40 million annual profit impact. The company then cut human support capacity too aggressively and had to start rebuilding it, because the system degraded on complex, ambiguous, and emotionally charged cases, and the institutional expertise to handle those had already walked out the door. The adaptable lesson is to segment the queue before you resize the team: automate the high-volume deterministic tier, then hold headcount on the ambiguous tier for at least two full quarters of production data before touching it. Deflection rate is a vanity metric if you are not also tracking resolution quality on the hardest 10% of contacts.

#Framework or mental model

The Coordination Trap: An essay published this week argues that AI project failure is systematically underreported not because individuals are dishonest but because no one can defect first. If an executive admits their AI gains are illusory, they embarrass peers and take on career risk. If everyone admitted it simultaneously, nobody would lose credibility, but no mechanism exists to coordinate that. The result is an organization where the public signal and the private belief have fully decoupled. The usable diagnostic is anonymous project sentiment polling: the author describes seeing half a team rate an initiative 3 out of 10 while the other half rated it 8 out of 10, and reads that bimodal split as direct evidence of suppressed information rather than genuine disagreement. Pair it with a ground-level adoption check, since many internal chatbot deployments show near-zero real uptake regardless of what the steering committee reports. Any leader running an AI portfolio can run both tests this quarter.

Sources:

  • Claude Fable 5 access changes
  • What's new in Claude Sonnet 5
  • SQLite Query Explainer
  • Tool: LLM cliché highlighter and the live tool
  • How Klarna's AI Agent Strategy Backfired But Became A Useful Lesson
  • Klarna AI assistant handles two-thirds of customer service chats in its first month
  • AI Mania Is Eviscerating Global Decision-Making

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • Apple: Apple emailed advertisers on July 14 about revised Advertising Services Terms of Service taking effect July 28. The contractual definition of where Apple Ads content may appear widened from Apple-owned apps and devices to a broader set of devices, operating systems, software, web applications and unspecified "other platforms or properties." This is the first documented case of Apple's own legal language describing ad surfaces it does not own. A separate Apple advertising policy effective July 14 sets Maps ad rules and bans home services categories (plumbing, HVAC, locksmith, roofing, pest control). Signal: the most privacy-positioned walled garden is quietly writing itself permission to sell demand off its own property. If Apple runs an off-platform network, the buy side gets a third large identity-rich demand source and the "privacy as product" narrative gets a lot more complicated to plan around.
  • Spotify: Six years after acquiring Megaphone, Spotify has fully absorbed the product into the Spotify Ad Server. Migration completed this month, VAST tags stopped working, and maximum ad duration moved from 60 to 90 seconds. Megaphone's Nielsen-based audience targeting and low-waterfall "Promotions" inventory were force-migrated too. Signal: acquisition is not integration, and the gap can run half a decade. The visible tell that a platform finally consolidated is when it kills the open standard (VAST) that let advertisers route around it. Every audio and video buyer who built workflows on Megaphone tags just had a dependency rewritten for them.
  • Zoom / Common Room: Zoom signed a definitive agreement on July 2 to acquire Common Room, an AI-native go-to-market intelligence platform that unifies CRM, product usage, marketing and engagement signals into person-level buyer profiles, with agents doing account research and outreach personalization. Close expected within weeks. Customers include Atlassian, Autodesk, Notion, Okta and Snowflake. Signal: buyer intelligence is being pulled inside the communications layer rather than sold as a standalone signal vendor. The category boundary between "where the conversation happens" and "who you should be talking to" is dissolving, which puts pressure on standalone intent-data vendors to become features.

#Category watch

GTM and revenue intelligence: This category is consolidating fast into adjacent platforms rather than growing as its own tier. Zoom absorbing Common Room, Marchex completing its Archenia acquisition on July 1 to fuse first-party call data with AI lead qualification, and Clari partnering with Salesloft on conversation-derived forecasting all point the same direction. The pattern: signal capture, signal interpretation, and signal action are collapsing into single vendors, because an agent that can research an account is only useful if it also sits where the outreach happens. For anyone building a martech org, the practical read is that the "best-of-breed intent vendor" slot in the stack is the one most likely to disappear into a platform renewal in the next 18 months.

#Stack intelligence

The strongest datapoint of the week is a negative one. Only about 34% of Salesforce customers have adopted Agentforce, roughly 23,000 of 150,000, and KeyBanc analysts attribute the gap to two things: enterprise data that is not clean, structured or connected, and deployments stuck in proof-of-concept rather than production. Deployment is not the bottleneck. Data readiness is.

This reframes the buy decision. The vendor layer has effectively finished shipping agentic capability. In the mid-July release wave alone, 6sense, OneSignal, Omneky and Wistia all shipped MCP servers, and dozens of vendors shipped autonomous agents across creative, research, lifecycle and service. Capability is now commodity and abundant. What is scarce is a data spine clean enough for an agent to act on without a human verifying every output.

The org-building implication: budget that would have gone to a third agentic point tool this year buys more if it goes to entity resolution, schema governance, and consent state consolidation. The companies moving fastest in 2027 will be the ones who did the unglamorous integration work in 2026, not the ones with the longest AI vendor list.

#Foundations concept of the day

Ad server and VAST: An ad server is the system that decides which specific creative to deliver into a given ad slot at request time, then logs the impression and the outcome. Publishers run one to manage their own inventory and direct-sold deals; advertisers run one to control creative and measure across the sites they buy. VAST (Video Ad Serving Template) is the open XML standard that lets a video or audio player on one company's platform call an ad from another company's ad server and understand the response: where the file is, how long it runs, which tracking pixels to fire. It matters at scale because VAST is what makes ad serving portable. If your creative and measurement run through VAST tags, you can move inventory and vendors without rebuilding your tracking. When a platform drops VAST support, as Spotify just did in folding Megaphone into its own ad server, every buyer on that platform loses the ability to serve and verify through their own stack and must trust the platform's numbers instead. Cross-industry example: this is the same dynamic that played out in mobile when app platforms moved measurement in-house, and in retail media where most networks report their own attribution with no independent serving path. The strategic question for a leader is not which ad server you use but how many of your channels can still be measured by a system you control.

#Watch list

  • Apple's off-property ad ambitions: The terms change lands July 28. Watch for any actual third-party placement, SDK, or DSP integration announcement in the following quarter. If it materializes, identity strategy for iOS-heavy audiences changes materially.
  • MCP servers as a martech distribution channel: The volume of vendors shipping MCP servers in a single release wave suggests the integration surface is shifting from API-and-dashboard to agent-queryable. Worth tracking whether buyers start evaluating vendors on agent accessibility rather than UI, because that would change how stacks get shortlisted.

Markets Signal

#Macro week in review

Canada. The TSX held up better than almost anything else on the board. Friday it slipped 76.30 points, or 0.22%, to close at 35,263.85, staying above the 35,000 line. The mix explains the resilience: energy names rallied hard on the oil spike while mining and banks dragged. For a Canadian carrier the index is only half the story. The Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25% on Wednesday, the sixth consecutive hold, and struck a relatively hawkish tone, flagging that the economy is recovering from a weak start to the year and that inflation will run above prior forecasts through 2026 before easing. USD/CAD sat near 1.4050 to 1.4060, close to a one month low for the pair, meaning a modestly stronger loonie. A stronger CAD trims the translated value of USD-denominated international ticket revenue, but it also trims the CAD cost of fuel and USD-denominated leases, which matters more this week than usual given what crude did.

United States. A broad risk-off week. The S&P 500 fell 1.55%, the Nasdaq 2.9%, and the Dow 0.93%. Friday alone the S&P 500 lost 1.01% to 7,457.69, the Nasdaq 1.40% to 25,520.24, and the Dow 406.55 points, or 0.77%, to 52,146.42. This was the S&P's first losing week in three and only its third since March. Two drivers: a semiconductor rout, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF down more than 4% on Friday, and renewed US and Iran escalation. Sector rotation was textbook defensive plus energy. Energy gained 4.7% on the week, REITs 2.2%, and consumer staples 1.27%, while tech and semis led the decline.

Asia. The worst of it. The Nikkei 225 fell 4.03% on Friday to 64,141.12 and posted its worst weekly loss since April 2025. The Shanghai Composite dropped 3.05% Friday to 3,764.155 and 5.81% on the week, with the Shenzhen Component down 8.9%. The Hang Seng fell 1.78% Friday to 24,562.24. Two forces stacked: the same AI spending and semiconductor valuation anxiety hitting the US, plus domestic liquidity pressure in China from upcoming mega-IPOs pulling cash out of the secondary market.

Oil and jet fuel. This is the line item that changes airline planning. WTI rose to $82.49 per barrel on July 17, up 4.48% in a single session and up more than 14% on the week, as the US reinstated a naval blockade near Iranian ports and Strait of Hormuz tanker traffic slowed to near halted. EIA's July Short-Term Energy Outlook noted refiners were holding jet fuel production alongside distillate to meet high global demand, which has kept the crack from blowing out even further, but a 14% weekly move in the feedstock is not something a hedging book absorbs quietly. Every carrier planning committee should be reworking Q4 fuel assumptions this week.

Rates and the consumer. The Fed is not riding to the rescue. Futures put roughly a 75% probability on a hold at 3.50% to 3.75%, with a modest tail pricing a hike rather than a cut, and implied odds of even one 25 basis point cut this year sitting near 20%. Inflation is the reason: CPI ran 4.2% year over year in May, and the Fed's preferred gauge came in at 4.1% headline with 3.4% core. Against that, the University of Michigan consumer sentiment print was the week's genuine upside surprise, rising to 54.4 in July versus a 51.0 expectation, a second straight monthly gain and the highest since February, helped by falling gasoline prices. All five components improved, with roughly 20% gains in durable goods buying conditions and year-ahead business expectations. One year inflation expectations eased to 4.2% from 4.6%. The catch: sentiment is still 12% below year ago levels, and the survey was taken before this week's oil spike works through to the pump.

The theme heading into next week. Consumer sentiment just improved on cheap gasoline, and gasoline is about to stop being cheap. That is a direct, mechanical threat to the discretionary travel demand curve in Q4. Pair it with a central bank on both sides of the border that has no room to cut, and the setup for travel and consumer discretionary is a demand signal that improved for a reason that is already reversing.

#MarTech & AdTech

  • Adobe, Salesforce, and HubSpot: The convergence story hardened rather than broke this week. All three are now positioning their platforms as infrastructure for AI agents rather than interfaces for human operators, with Adobe having rebranded Experience Cloud toward an agent-first CX posture. The distinction between martech, adtech, and sales tech is collapsing into one addressable surface, which means procurement decisions made on category logic are now buying overlapping capability.
  • The Trade Desk and Adobe: The Real-Time CDP integration lets advertisers activate first-party data across channels including CTV without leaving the Adobe stack. The signal is that the demand side is being pulled into the customer data layer rather than the reverse. For anyone in an Adobe shop, this deepens the gravity well: the more activation runs through the native integration, the harder the identity and audience layer is to move later.

#AI models & APIs

  • Moonshot AI, Kimi K3: The week's defining event. Moonshot released Kimi K3 on Friday, a 2.8 trillion parameter open weights model, the largest open weight release to date, claiming benchmark performance trailing only Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 on overall capability, at a fraction of the cost. Markets treated it as a second DeepSeek moment. IG's Tony Sycamore estimated $314 billion was wiped from valuation estimates for the two unlisted US labs. The strategic implication is not that Chinese labs caught up, it is that frontier-adjacent capability is now downloadable and self-hostable. Any enterprise AI roadmap built on the assumption that top-tier inference will stay expensive and API-gated needs rerunning.
  • Open weights as a pricing floor: The market reaction repriced the AI trade by layer, not uniformly. Model providers selling access got hit. Anyone whose business assumes cheap, abundant inference got a tailwind. That split is the useful frame for the next several quarters.

#Travel & airline tech

  • Amadeus, the look-to-book crisis: Both Amadeus and Sabre have now pointed to a possible future of up to 200,000 searches per ticket sold as agentic AI shoppers flood distribution systems with fare queries. Amadeus is answering with precomputed fare caching and an Advanced Airline Profile filtering layer that uses machine learning to block unactionable NDC search traffic before it reaches airline systems. Early results cut unproductive traffic by more than 70% in some cases, and Air France-KLM reported the solution blocked the majority of irrelevant traffic to its systems. This is the most underrated infrastructure problem in airline digital right now. Agentic shopping is a cost-per-search problem long before it is a conversion opportunity.
  • Amadeus and Microsoft, agentic airline operations: Their joint airline agentic AI whitepaper argues agents are production-ready across rebooking, commerce, marketing, turnaround management, and service. Trials show an agent identifying a booking, parsing a verbal change request, proposing options, articulating the fare differential, and initiating payment across multiple languages. The gating factor named in the work is governance, not capability.
  • Amadeus versus Sabre: The competitive fight escalated, with Sabre's CEO accusing Amadeus of holding a dominant monopoly position and signalling regulatory and legal avenues, while Amadeus argues its footprint now spans retailing, biometric identity, hospitality, and payments. Distribution leverage is becoming a regulatory question, not just a commercial one.
  • Air Canada and Club Avolta: Aeroplan members can now earn points on eligible purchases at more than 900 airport retail locations operated by Hudson and Dufry, at one point per C$2 spent, expanding later in 2026 to HMSHost food and beverage for nearly 1,900 total locations. Earning extends through Avolta's Reserve and Collect and the Club Avolta app. The signal: loyalty currency is being pushed into the physical airport dwell window, where intent is high and the airline previously had no earn surface.

#AI Infrastructure Stack

Raw materials & hardware

  • Critical minerals repricing: All 18 tracked rare earth elements rose in July, averaging a 16.7% gain, led by germanium up 27.8%, indium up 26.5%, and dysprosium up 25.4%. Gallium hit $288.82 per kg on the SMM industrial benchmark on July 1, up 4.2% from June, while the China FOB export price held near $400 per kg for a third straight month. That gap is the tell: export licensing, not geology, is the binding constraint. China's January catalogue update added samarium, gadolinium, and lutetium controls, and the current export-control reprieve expires November 10, 2026, which sets up a potential physical scarcity event in ex-China markets before Western supply reaches commercial scale.

Chips & semiconductors

  • TSMC: Record quarter, punished anyway. Net income surged 77% on record revenue, quarterly sales up 36%, June monthly revenue around NT$442 billion, up 67.9% year over year. Shares still fell 7.3% in Taipei after the company raised both spending and revenue projections. Raising capex is now read as a risk signal rather than a confidence signal, which is a meaningful shift in how the market is underwriting the AI buildout.
  • ASML: Raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to EUR 43 to 45 billion from EUR 36 to 40 billion, the second increase this year, on AI chip demand. The equipment layer is still seeing orders that contradict the demand-doubt narrative in the equity tape.
  • Memory versus foundry divergence: Memory names led Asian tech lower on oversupply concerns and profit taking, while AI-serving foundries held on long-term demand. HBM supply, which Nvidia and AMD depend on through suppliers like SK Hynix, is being priced as a commodity cycle again rather than a structural shortage.
  • Intel: Became the first company to ship high-volume logic using ASML High-NA EUV scanners, alongside reported yield improvement on 18A. A credible second leading-edge source changes the negotiating position of every large accelerator buyer.

Cooling & energy

  • Nvidia's closed-loop liquid cooling: Newest AI servers move fully to liquid cooling using a recirculated water and propylene glycol coolant running hot, which Nvidia says eliminates large amounts of power usage and effectively all water usage. Water permitting has become a siting constraint in several jurisdictions, so removing it is as much a regulatory unlock as an efficiency one.
  • Rack-level physics is the new bottleneck: The Data Center Insights conference on July 15 and 16 centered on liquid cooling chemistry, 800VDC power architecture for megawatt-class racks, and 800G fiber validation. Roughly 76% of AI servers are expected to be liquid-cooled in 2026, and the liquid cooling market is around $3.7 billion this year. Facilities without liquid cooling already installed are not competitive for current-generation deployments.
  • Virginia's data center power tax: A consumption levy of $0.011 per kilowatt-hour on all data center electricity took effect July 1, expected to raise roughly $600 million annually. The first serious sign that jurisdictions will monetize AI load rather than simply court it. Expect the model to travel.
  • Nuclear as baseload strategy: The pattern set by Microsoft's roughly $1 billion, 20-year Constellation PPA for 835 MW from Three Mile Island Unit 1, and extended by Google's Kairos Power SMR agreement, is now the default hyperscaler playbook. AI data centers are projected to push US data center power demand from roughly 176 TWh today to 325 to 580 TWh by 2028, and nuclear is the only always-on zero-carbon source at that scale.

Data centers & cloud capex

  • Hyperscaler capex guidance keeps climbing: Forecasts for 2026 hyperscaler AI capital spending were raised toward the $750 billion range from roughly $670 billion, with Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, and Alphabet collectively guiding to north of $710 billion combined and projections crossing $1 trillion in 2027. The capex commitment is going up in the same week the equity market punished the companies making the commitment.

Stack insight

The stack split in two this week and the split is the story. Physical layers, foundry, lithography, cooling, and power, are reporting record demand and raising guidance. The financial layer is repricing risk downward on the same news. Kimi K3 is the hinge: if frontier-adjacent capability is open weights and cheap to run, the value of proprietary model access falls while the value of compute, power, and cooling to run inference everywhere rises. The 12 to 18 month constraint is not chips. It is interconnection queues, megawatt-rack thermal design, and licensed access to gallium, germanium, and heavy rare earths ahead of the November 10 expiry. Whoever locked power and cooling in 2025 will ship in 2027. Whoever is still negotiating a grid interconnect will not, regardless of how many accelerators they can buy.

#Funding rounds worth noting

  • Fireworks AI, $1.505 billion Series D: Tooling for enterprises to turn general-purpose models into specialized intelligence trained on their own data. The size of this round is the market pricing the exact thesis Kimi K3 validated: the durable value is in adapting models to proprietary data, not in owning the base model.
  • Helsing, $1.8 billion: Led by JPMorgan Chase, Lightspeed, and Iconiq. Defense AI at a scale that now competes with frontier labs for capital and talent.
  • Together AI, $800 million Series C: Led by Aramco Ventures at an $8.3 billion post-money valuation. Infrastructure for running open source models, funded by an energy major. That investor pairing tells you where both open weights and power converge.
  • AIsphere, $439 million Series C: Led by Alibaba, closed July 14.
  • Chai Discovery, $400 million Series C: Led by Index, Kleiner Perkins, and Sequoia.
  • 8090 Solutions, $135 million: Led by Salesforce. A platform for building enterprise software with coordinated AI agents under human oversight, which is Salesforce buying optionality on the agent-built-software thesis rather than building it internally.

#M&A signal

Deal flow this week was concentrated outside the AI application layer. American Industrial Partners agreed to take Avanos Medical private in an all-cash deal valued near $1.272 billion, and GH Power, a clean-energy and critical-materials company, is going public via combination with Matinas BioPharma. No major MarTech or AdTech acquisition landed. The more interesting consolidation signal is negative: with the Google and HubSpot combination having already collapsed under antitrust pressure, the large platforms are pursuing integration and minority investment rather than acquisition. Adobe and The Trade Desk partnering instead of merging, and Salesforce leading a round rather than buying the company, are the same behaviour. Category consolidation is still happening, it is just being executed through partnership and equity stakes because the regulatory path for outright purchase is closed.

#The week's big bet

The week's biggest bet was not made by a buyer, it was made by Moonshot giving away a 2.8 trillion parameter model. Releasing frontier-adjacent capability as open weights is a bet that the value in AI migrates from model access to everything required to run models at scale, which is precisely the layer where capex kept climbing even as equities sold off. The market read it immediately, wiping an estimated $314 billion from US lab valuations while energy, REITs, and the physical infrastructure stack held or gained. For digital leaders in travel and MarTech, the implication is concrete: any vendor contract, roadmap, or business case that assumes premium model access is the scarce input is now built on a melting assumption. The scarce inputs are proprietary data, the ability to serve inference cheaply, and the governance to let agents transact. Spend the next planning cycle securing those, and stop paying a premium for a capability that just became downloadable.

Landscape Scan

#The convergence watch (loyalty data → media networks)

  • Delta, June-quarter earnings (Jul 13): Loyalty-related revenue up 19% year over year, with American Express remuneration at $2.4B for the quarter and full-year 2026 guidance of $9B, up 10% on 2025. Card spend has now grown double digits for seven consecutive quarters, concentrated in premium Reserve holders. What it signals: the co-brand channel is still the highest-margin monetization of loyalty data at scale, and it sets the revenue bar any airline media network has to beat before it earns real board attention. (Benzinga transcript, Investing.com transcript)
  • United, second-quarter results (Jul 15, call Jul 16): Total revenue $17.7B, up 16%. Loyalty revenue up 11%, a second-quarter record for new co-brand card accounts at plus 22%, card spend plus 14%, MileagePlus enrollments plus 9%. Notably, Kinective Media was not broken out as a disclosed revenue line. What it signals: the airline that built the category's first media network is still reporting the loyalty story through the card, not the ad business. Media network revenue remains strategically loud and financially quiet, which is the honest state of the category. (Yahoo Finance call highlights, AeroTime)
  • Myer launches an in-house media network off MYER one (Jul 16): Australian department store Myer stood up the Myer Media Network, built on MYER one loyalty data and omnichannel touchpoints, with an AI-native sponsored product layer from Mirakl Ads, and hired Michael Sharlassian to run it. What it signals: the loyalty-program-to-media-network playbook is now being executed by mid-cap retailers with a few million members, not just 100M-member carriers. The scale threshold for a defensible network is falling, which compresses the window in which "we are too small for this" is a credible answer. (Mi3, ContentGrip)
  • Trend line, not this week: The demand-side plumbing that makes travel loyalty data sellable keeps consolidating. Marriott put Bonvoy segments into a self-serve model via The Trade Desk in mid-June, monetizing a roughly 237M-member graph with 200-plus targetable attributes across roughly 9,500 properties. United and Marriott have been jointly pitching advertisers on in-trip targeting across seatback and in-room screens since March. Kinective Media is also selling inventory on behalf of JetBlue, meaning one carrier is now an ad sales house for another. Watch whether a second carrier signs onto Kinective rather than building its own. (AdExchanger, Skift, Adweek)

#Airline loyalty & digital

  • Lufthansa Group: Miles & More will be renamed Lufthansa Group Miles & More by end of 2026, consolidating branding across group carriers including ITA Airways. What it signals: group-level loyalty consolidation as the integration lever. When a program becomes the group brand rather than the airline brand, the data asset is being centralized ahead of any monetization play. (Upgraded Points, week of Jul 14-18)
  • JetBlue: Partnered with ClarityPay to offer installment payment at checkout, with the lowest available plan surfaced inline. By year end, TrueBlue points will accrue incrementally as installments are paid rather than at purchase. What it signals: points earn is being decoupled from the transaction moment and re-attached to the payment schedule. That turns the loyalty ledger into a repayment engagement loop and creates a new behavioral data stream tied to credit posture, not just travel intent. (Upgraded Points)
  • Canada, watch item: AIR MILES completes its transition to BMO's Blue Rewards this summer, collapsing Cash and Dream Miles into a single balance at 1,500 points equals $10, moving travel fulfillment onto Expedia Group, and adding Porter Airlines, Accor, Instacart and MTY as partners while Shell Canada exits to Scene+. What it signals: the Canadian coalition layer is being rebuilt around bank-owned currency with an OTA fulfillment backend. Coalition programs are becoming bank distribution assets, and Porter is quietly buying reach through someone else's coalition rather than scaling VIPorter alone. (Prince of Travel, Milesopedia)

#Hotel & travel loyalty

  • Hilton Honors: Program terms and conditions updated effective Jul 15, covering Yotel joining Honors, event planner earning, and points purchase rules. What it signals: brand-count expansion remains the cheapest way to grow a member graph, and every new brand added is more inventory and more attribute depth for a future media offer. (LoyaltyLobby)
  • Marriott Bonvoy: New "Exclusive For You" targeted member offers went live Jul 15, valid through Oct 31. What it signals: the same first-party segmentation Marriott sells to advertisers is being run against its own P&L first. Targeted internal offers are the proof-of-concept that de-risks selling the segments externally. (LoyaltyLobby)

#AdTech & retail media

  • Netflix, second-quarter results (Jul 16): Ad revenue tracking to roughly $3B in 2026, roughly double 2025. Management confirmed programmatic access to Pause Ads and live sports inventory opening this summer, with The Trade Desk, Amazon DSP and Google DV360 as partners. Amazon shopping audiences are already usable against Netflix inventory via Amazon DSP in the US and across EMEA. Shares fell about 8% on softer forward guidance. What it signals: commerce and loyalty audiences are now routable into premium CTV through standard DSP workflows. For a carrier, that means first-party segments have a credible high-attention destination beyond owned screens, which materially improves the business case for packaging loyalty data as addressable inventory. (PPC Land, eMarketer)

#Loyalty tech vendors

  • Plusgrade / Points (announced Jul 7): Launched Buy BreezePoints with Breeze Airways on its Loyalty Currency Retailing platform, extending an existing ancillary relationship that already covered Preferred Seating, Extra Legroom and Seat Blocker into loyalty currency sales. What it signals: the vendor land grab is happening at the currency layer, not the engine layer. Plusgrade is bundling ancillary and points retailing into one commercial relationship, which makes a later rip-and-replace of the loyalty stack considerably harder. Build-vs-buy read: buy the currency retailing, keep the member graph and identity resolution in house. (PR Newswire, Runway Girl Network)

#Strategic implication

The two biggest US carriers reported this week and the loyalty story in both was the credit card, not the media network. United, which owns the category's first-mover asset, still did not break Kinective out as a line item while its co-brand accounts hit a Q2 record. Meanwhile a mid-cap Australian retailer stood up a loyalty-fed media network in a week. The strategic question for a CDO or VP Digital at a major carrier is no longer whether to build a media network, it is whether the member graph is clean enough to be sold twice, once to a bank as co-brand remuneration and once to advertisers as addressable inventory, without the two propositions eroding each other. The forcing function is identity: with Amazon and Trade Desk audiences now routing into premium CTV as standard workflow, a carrier that cannot resolve its members to an addressable ID will end up renting reach from the same platforms it hoped to compete with.

item.title: The Platero Brief, No. 23: Sunday, July 19, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Executive Pulse

#Macro signal

The AI buildout is now embedded in the inflation math, and that changes the rate calculus: Post-earnings weakness this week was driven by a "three-headed" pullback, a chip sell-off (the semiconductor index sliding toward 20% off its highs), oil breaking above $80 on Middle East tension, and a 10%-plus Netflix drop. But the durable signal underneath is that the cost of the AI capex supercycle is now showing up in the CPI itself, even as broader inflation data stayed reassuring enough that no rate hike is expected this month. Strategically, this reframes AI spend: it is no longer a discretionary line item that gets cut when rates rise, it is a structural cost input that regulators and central banks are starting to watch. For tech, product, and marketing leaders, the implication is that budgets for AI infrastructure should be defended as fixed operating cost, not tested against every quarter's macro mood. Concentration risk is the other side: a market this dependent on a handful of chip and platform names means one earnings miss moves the whole index.

#Tech industry

  • Hg Capital's $6.4B all-cash take-private of OneStream: A classic PE play for corporate performance management software sold into finance departments. Strategic implication: the finance-software layer is being consolidated under patient private capital precisely as CFOs become the internal owners of AI governance and spend discipline. Expect the tools that finance teams use to plan, forecast, and control AI budgets to get bundled and repriced. Buyers should assume roadmap and pricing volatility on CPM platforms over the next 18 months.

#AI at the leadership level

The EU AI Act's high-risk obligations were quietly deferred from August 2, 2026 to December 2027 under the Digital Omnibus, but the Article 50 transparency rules were not deferred and still land on August 2. That means any customer-facing system must disclose when a user is interacting with AI, on schedule, in weeks. The board-level read: the hard compliance cliff moved, but the reputational and disclosure floor did not. Meanwhile the governance gap is stark. Deloitte finds AI is now on 69% of board agendas (up from 55%), yet only about 39% of Fortune 100 boards have any explicit AI oversight mechanism, and a majority of enterprises run AI in production with no designated leadership owner. The move that matters: name an accountable executive for AI now, before the transparency deadline forces the question in public.

#Leadership & org design

The strongest signal in operating-model design this quarter is the collapse of the management pyramid. Because one human can supervise far more agent output than human output, spans of control are widening and the pure-manager layer is thinning. BCG's 2026 work reports organizations that redesign the operating model around AI, rather than bolting AI onto the existing chart, are seeing up to 60% cost reduction and 80% cycle-time reduction. PwC frames the same shift as the "rise of the generalist," broader outcome-owning roles replacing narrow functional ones. The practical takeaway for leaders: the win is not headcount cuts, it is redrawing the "work chart" around outcomes and treating agents as first-class org units with named human owners.

#Question worth asking your team this week

If a regulator or a customer asked us today who is personally accountable for our AI systems, could we name that person, and does their authority actually match the risk we have in production?

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • Framer external agents: Framer just opened its canvas to Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Gemini CLI. Copy the prompt from framer.com/agents/external, run one terminal command, and the agent gets direct read/write access to your canvas, components, and CMS with no manual MCP setup. Setup is 5-10 minutes and it works on the editor, not the live site, so nothing publishes until you say so. Best first job: point it at a CMS collection and have it do bulk content edits, localization, or redirects that would take a person an afternoon.
  • Context audit on your longest automation: The practical finding making the rounds this week is that model reasoning starts degrading around 3,000 tokens, well below the technical max, with a sweet spot near 150-300 words per task. Before shipping any multi-step prompt or agent, log the full context payload at each turn and cut anything that does not need to be there right now. Trim your three longest production prompts and watch quality and cost both improve.
  • Meeting-to-action extraction: Drop a raw transcript or recording into an assistant and prompt "Summarize the decisions made, the open questions, and the action items by owner." It is one of the highest-leverage 20-minute habits available and almost nobody outside of tech has adopted it. Standardize the exact wording across your team so the output is consistent enough to paste straight into a tracker.

#Case study worth stealing

Lightspeed Commerce, autonomous support at 99% coverage: The e-commerce and fintech platform routed its Intercom Fin agent into 99% of support conversations and let it autonomously resolve up to 65% of them. The move was not "add a chatbot," it was making the agent the default first touch on every ticket and measuring resolution rate rather than deflection. A digital team can steal the framing: pick one high-volume support or ops queue, put an agent on 100% of intake as triage, and hold it to an autonomous-resolution number instead of a vanity deflection metric.

#Framework or mental model

Loop engineering: Instead of writing the perfect prompt each time, you design the system that prompts the agent for you, made of scheduled automations, isolated worktrees, codified skills, connectors to real tools, and a subagent that independently verifies the output, with progress stored in an external file so it survives between runs. The named risk is "cognitive surrender," taking whatever the loop returns without an opinion. Digital leaders can apply it to any recurring deliverable (weekly reports, competitor scans, content drafts) by building the loop once and reviewing outputs with judgment rather than restarting from a blank prompt daily.

#Rabbit hole

GEO is now a measured discipline, not a buzzword: At least eight generative-engine-optimization platforms now exist to track how often a brand appears in AI answers, and the tactics have hardened into something a team can execute. Write for citability with clean headers, concise paragraphs, and FAQ patterns so an answer engine can lift a clean response. Distributing the same content across many trusted publications reportedly lifts AI citations up to 325% versus publishing only on your own site. Platform choice matters: 97% of Perplexity answers cite sources versus 16% for ChatGPT, so the surface you optimize for changes the play. The metric to adopt is Share of Model Voice, how often your brand shows up in AI answers relative to competitors, because ranking on Google no longer means being visible where a growing share of buyers now ask.

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • Zoom / Common Room: Zoom signed a definitive deal (announced early July, closing within weeks) to acquire Common Room, an AI-native go-to-market intelligence platform whose RoomieAI agents unify first-party CRM, product, and engagement signals into person-level buyer profiles and act on them. Common Room's roster includes Atlassian, Anthropic, Okta, and Snowflake. Signal: a communications platform is buying its way into the revenue-data layer. The battleground is no longer "who stores the data" but "who owns the agent that acts on the signal," and adjacent-category players are willing to pay to get there.
  • BlueConic / Blueshift: BlueConic closed its acquisition of Blueshift, bolting cross-channel decisioning (email, push, in-app, SMS, web) onto its first-party profile engine. The combined base is 600-plus customers across CPG, retail, DTC, and travel and hospitality (ASICS, L'Oreal, StitchFix, Five Below). Signal: this is explicitly framed as building an agentic CDP, not a data-consolidation play. The CDP category is moving from "unify and store" to "decide and execute" in a single vendor.
  • Databricks / CustomerLake: Databricks' agentic CDP, launched at Data + AI Summit and now in private preview with HP, Circle K, and AB InBev, folds identity resolution, audience building, activation, and "infinity campaigns" (continuous agentic loops) directly into the lakehouse under Unity Catalog governance. Signal: the data-cloud vendors are collapsing the martech stack into the warehouse itself. If the profile, the model, and the activation all live where the data already sits, the standalone CDP's reason to exist narrows.

#Category watch

Agentic CDPs: Three moves in roughly a month (Zoom/Common Room, BlueConic/Blueshift, Databricks/CustomerLake) point at the same shift. The 2018-era CDP promise was unification, get every customer signal into one profile. The 2026 promise is action, put an agent on top of that profile that builds the audience, picks the next-best move, and activates across channels on a loop. For anyone building a martech org, the buying question is changing from "which CDP unifies our data best" to "where does the decisioning agent live, and do we trust it inside the warehouse, inside a point solution, or as a layer we assemble ourselves."

#Stack intelligence

The consolidation pattern to watch is the warehouse-native stack. When Databricks embeds a CDP inside the lakehouse and governs it with the same catalog that governs everything else, the enterprise buy-vs-build math flips. A team that already runs its data platform on a lakehouse or a cloud warehouse can now treat the customer data layer as a feature of infrastructure it already owns, rather than a six-figure standalone contract with its own identity model, its own governance, and its own copy of the data. The architectural tell is data gravity: activation is moving to where the first-party data already lives instead of the data being shipped out to a marketing tool. Point-solution CDPs counter by racing to add agents and execution faster than the warehouses can add marketing polish. For an org-builder, the near-term call is less "which tool" and more "how many copies of the customer profile do we want to maintain, and who governs them."

#Foundations concept of the day

Data clean rooms: A clean room is a secure, neutral environment where two parties (say a retailer and a brand, or an advertiser and a publisher) can match and analyze their combined data without either side ever seeing the other's raw customer records. Each party uploads its first-party data, the room matches individuals on a shared key like a hashed email, and both sides get aggregate results (overlap size, campaign reach, conversions) rather than row-level identities. It matters at scale because third-party cookies are gone and no single replacement ID won, so the durable way to connect audiences across companies is privacy-safe collaboration on first-party data. Real example: a consumer-goods brand runs a campaign on a retailer's media network, then uses the retailer's clean room to see which ad-exposed shoppers actually bought, without the retailer handing over its customer list or the brand exposing its own. Vendors like Optable now run live Chrome-auction campaigns and attribution through this model, a sign the clean room has moved from privacy insurance to standard media plumbing.

#Watch list

  • Warehouse-native CDPs vs point-solution CDPs: watch whether enterprise buyers standardize on the customer data layer their data cloud already offers (Databricks, and expect a Snowflake response) or keep the marketer-friendly standalone CDP as a separate agentic execution layer. The next 12 months decide whether the CDP is a product category or a warehouse feature.
  • The post-Sandbox identity portfolio: with Google's Privacy Sandbox wound down and no single cookie replacement, the 2026 identity stack is a portfolio (UID2, ID5, RampID, clean-room matches, first-party and contextual signals). Watch for tooling that abstracts across these IDs so buyers do not have to bet on one, that abstraction layer is where the next durable adtech position gets built.

Markets Signal

#Macro pulse

Markets are closed for the weekend, so this reads off Friday's closes and a rough week. Two forces dominated: a China-AI shock and a Middle East oil spike. Canada: the S&P/TSX composite slipped about 0.2% to roughly 35,340 Friday, whipsawed as energy gains offset a global chip selloff and softer gold. USD/CAD sat near 1.40, essentially flat on the day and below the 0.5% flag, so no material hit to Canadian carrier international revenue for now. USA: the S&P 500 fell 1% to 7,475, the Dow lost 0.8% to 52,146, and the Nasdaq dropped 1.4% to 25,520, with all three down on the week (Nasdaq off 2.9%) as semiconductors got smoked. The Bank of Canada held at 2.25% on July 15 for a sixth straight hold, flagging CPI at 3.2% in May driven by war-linked gasoline, with core near 2%. Asia led the rout: Nikkei crashed 4% to 64,141, Shanghai fell 3.1%, Hang Seng lost 1.8%. Oil: WTI surged about 4.5% to $82.49, well past the 2% flag, up roughly 12% on the week on the Iran conflict.

#Today's industry move

The week's defining move was risk-off in tech, not a single deal. Chinese lab Moonshot released Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model, triggering a DeepSeek-style repricing of the "more compute equals more value" thesis. TSMC fell 7% Friday despite a 77% jump in quarterly operating profit, SoftBank dropped 9%, and Nvidia briefly ceded the most-valuable-company crown to Apple. On the deal side, Zoom acquired go-to-market intelligence startup Common Room (terms undisclosed), folding CRM plus product-usage signals and AI outreach agents into its stack, a signal that signal-based, AI-native GTM tooling keeps commanding premium multiples.

#AI infrastructure watch

The selloff hit the physical stack hardest. AMD fell 5%, Intel 4%, and Nvidia slid 3% before partly recovering as capital rotated out of AI chips. The trigger was fear that cheaper open-weight models let hyperscalers scale back capex, compressing the demand curve that premium silicon valuations are priced against. TSMC compounded it by guiding to higher-than-expected capex on rising tool prices, feeding margin-compression worries across the supply chain. This is the first serious market test of whether the app-layer efficiency story undercuts the infrastructure buildout.

#Signal or noise?

Part of a larger trend: the second China-model shock in eighteen months means the "compute is destiny" premium now reprices on every efficiency breakthrough, and the oil leg is a genuine conflict-driven repricing, not a blip.

#Watch tomorrow

Watch Monday's open in Asia and North America for whether the chip rout stabilizes or cascades, and track WTI, if the Iran conflict keeps crude above $80 into next week, jet-fuel-exposed carriers and Canadian CPI both feel it, though a higher oil complex cushions the TSX energy weighting.

item.title: The Platero Brief, No. 22: Saturday, July 18, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Executive Pulse

#Macro signal

A demand-side scare hit AI infrastructure, and geopolitics compounded it: A Chinese lab (Moonshot) shipping a frontier-class open-weight model on the same week custom silicon began displacing some Nvidia demand flipped the market's AI anxiety from "can we make enough chips" to "will this spending pay off." More than $1 trillion in chip market value was wiped in the selloff, while renewed US-Iran strikes pushed oil back above $80 and sent markets risk-off. Why it matters: the era of unquestioned AI capex is being priced with more skepticism. Leaders should expect their own boards to start asking for proof of return on AI spend, not just proof of activity.

#Tech industry

  • AI competition went global and cheaper in one week: Moonshot's Kimi K3 matched or beat several leading US models on benchmarks at open-weight pricing. Strategic implication: model capability is commoditizing faster than most 2026 plans assumed. Any strategy premised on a durable capability moat from a single vendor is now fragile, and the smart posture is model-portability by design.
  • The value is moving to implementation: Anthropic and Blackstone are backing "Ode," and OpenAI stood up a deployment arm, both betting that the next trillion-dollar AI business is helping enterprises actually deploy, not just supplying models. Implication: the scarce resource is not the model, it is the org's ability to rewire workflows around it.

#AI at the leadership level

Nearly three quarters of CEOs now say they are the primary decision-maker on AI, double last year's share, yet most still cannot prove clear financial returns. That gap between personal ownership and provable ROI is the defining executive tension of mid-2026. The risk is a wave of CEO-driven initiatives with no operating-model change underneath them, which is exactly the pattern that produces expensive pilots and no P&L impact.

#Leadership & org design

The sharper CEOs are sorting into three postures worth self-diagnosing against: Followers run isolated edge experiments with no enterprise narrative, Pragmatists pursue ROI-driven pilots but stay stuck use-case by use-case, and Trailblazers use AI to redesign whole workflows and business models end to end. The distinction that predicts results is not spend, it is whether AI is bolted onto the existing operating model or used to redraw it. Half of CEOs now report running a hybrid model strategy (foundation, custom, and small specialized models chosen by task), which is the practical signature of the Trailblazer posture.

#Question worth asking your team this week

If a competitor could license the same models we use tomorrow, what in our operating model, not our tech stack, would still be hard for them to copy?

Practitioner Pulse

#Try this now

  • 6sense MCP Server (open beta): 6sense put its account intelligence, predictive buying stages, and keyword intent behind an MCP endpoint, so any MCP-compatible agent (Claude, ChatGPT) can call it directly. If you run ABM or lifecycle, this is the pattern to copy: stop exporting intent data into dashboards nobody opens and instead make it callable inside the agent your team already works in. Worth 20 minutes to see whether your own intent signals could be exposed the same way.
  • Superhuman Docs on Coda: A single prompt spins up a campaign hub with tasks, calendars, dashboards, and live Jira or Salesforce data pulled in. The useful move is not the doc, it is treating the brief as the interface. Give it your next campaign as one paragraph and see how much of the scaffolding it builds before a human touches it.
  • Claude Sonnet 5: Stronger coding, tool use, and debugging at a lower token price. For anyone running agentic workflows or internal tools, the price drop matters more than the benchmark: task-routing to a cheaper capable model is where the real cost savings landed this month, not in the flashiest frontier release.

#Case study worth stealing

Adore Me, content operations rebuilt around governed AI: The retailer cut stylist note-writing time by 36%, took product description generation from 20 hours to 20 minutes per batch, and compressed localized launch time from months to 10 days, while non-branded SEO traffic rose 40%. The adaptable part is not the tooling, it is the shape: structured source material feeding a model, brand voice rules as guardrails, human review at the end, and a clear business metric on the other side. Any digital team sitting on a large content backlog can copy that four-part frame this quarter.

#Framework or mental model

Personalization at scale is a coordination problem, not a creative one: The lesson from Cadbury's hyperlocal Diwali work (ads featuring 2,000-plus local stores) is that scaled personalization needs four things working together: clean data, localization logic, approval rules, and distribution coordination. The model output is the easy 10%. Digital leaders should audit which of those four they are missing before blaming the AI for underwhelming personalization.

AI Stack Daily

#Vendor & platform moves

  • 6sense: Launched its MCP Server in open beta, exposing account insights, predictive buying stages, and keyword intent as callable tools for any MCP-compatible agent. Signal: The intelligence layer of the stack is repositioning from dashboard to callable service. Vendors that sell "insight" now have to be consumable by an agent, not just a human, and the ones that ship an MCP endpoint first will get embedded into buyers' agent workflows before competitors are even considered.
  • BlueConic + Blueshift: BlueConic acquired Blueshift, folding a CDP together with decision and campaign intelligence. Signal: Consolidation is moving up the stack. Standalone data collection and standalone activation are both being pulled into single platforms, because a customer data layer with no decisioning attached is losing its reason to exist as a separate line item.
  • Zoom + Common Room: Zoom acquired go-to-market intelligence startup Common Room. Signal: Communications platforms are buying their way into revenue intelligence, another sign the category lines between conversation tools, signal capture, and GTM data are dissolving.

#Category watch

AI-native MarTech valuations vs legacy: AI-native martech firms are commanding more than 2x the multiple of traditional vendors, reaching 7.8x revenue in M&A, while median venture funding sizes keep compressing (around $3M and trending down). The category is bifurcating: a small set of AI-native platforms absorbing premium capital and acquisitions, and a long tail of legacy tools being bought for parts or repriced down. Anyone building or rationalizing a stack should assume the mid-tier point solution is the most endangered species.

#Stack intelligence

The through-line across today's moves is that the stack is reorganizing around agents as the primary consumer of data, not people. When 6sense makes intent callable and buyers wire it into Claude or ChatGPT, the value shifts from the UI to the API surface. Enterprises rebuilding stacks right now should weight one question heavily in every buy decision: can an agent call this system's intelligence directly, or does it trap value behind a human-only interface? Tools that fail that test become integration debt within a year.

#Foundations concept of the day

MCP (Model Context Protocol): An open standard that lets an AI model call external tools and data sources through a common interface, the way USB lets any device plug into any port. Instead of custom-coding each integration, a vendor exposes an "MCP server" and any MCP-compatible agent can query it. Why it matters at scale: it collapses integration cost and makes your data assets directly consumable by the agents your teams use. Real example: 6sense's new MCP server means a marketer can ask their agent "which accounts are in-market for X" and get a live answer without ever opening the 6sense dashboard. The strategic implication is that every data vendor now competes on how cleanly it plugs into the agent layer.

#Watch list

  • Whether Salesforce, Adobe, and HubSpot ship first-party MCP servers for their core clouds. The one that makes its data callable first sets the default integration path for enterprise agents.
  • AI-native CDP and decisioning combinations following the BlueConic + Blueshift template. Expect at least one more data-plus-decisioning tie-up this quarter.

Markets Signal

#Macro pulse

  • Canada: S&P/TSX Composite slipped 0.2% to 35,340, dragged by mining and banks as gold fell and rate-cut hopes cooled. USD/CAD held roughly steady, with the bigger swing factor being oil strength supporting Canadian energy names even as the broad index dipped.
  • USA: Broad selloff. S&P 500 fell 1.02% to 7,457, Nasdaq dropped 1.40% to 25,520, Dow lost 0.77% to 52,146. All three posted weekly losses (Nasdaq down about 2.9% on the week). The driver was a semiconductor rout plus a risk-off geopolitical mood. Energy was the only sector to gain; communications and consumer cyclicals were hit hardest, with Netflix plunging on earnings.
  • Asia: Risk-off tone carried through global tech as news of a Chinese frontier AI model rattled US chip names, pressuring the broader tech complex.
  • Oil: WTI jumped about 4.5% to roughly $82, a one-month high, on a sixth straight night of US strikes against Iran and Red Sea shipping-disruption fears. A sustained move above $80 pressures airline fuel costs directly and is the single most important line for travel operators to watch.

#Today's industry move

Netflix plunged on its earnings print, leading a communications-sector drop and reinforcing that even the strongest streaming and platform names are being repriced when growth or spend expectations wobble. For digital leaders, the signal is that the market is done paying for spend without proof of return.

#AI infrastructure watch

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index has fallen more than 13% in a month, and today's leg down erased over $1 trillion in combined AI-chip value. Two forces converged: custom silicon from major tech firms began shipping in volume, contesting Nvidia's near-monopoly, and Moonshot's Kimi K3 (2.8 trillion parameters, the largest open-weight model yet) matched or beat several US models at open pricing. AMD fell about 5%, Intel about 4%, Nvidia about 3% before paring losses. The anxiety flipped from chip supply to spending sustainability in a single session.

#Signal or noise?

Signal. This is not a one-day blip: it is the market repricing the entire AI capex thesis around cheaper open-weight competition and custom silicon eroding pricing power, a theme that will run for quarters, not days.

#Watch tomorrow

Whether oil holds above $80 into next week. A sustained crude rally on Iran escalation would hit airline margins and consumer discretionary demand at the same time.
